choices: プラスチックはすべて使うのをやめるべきだ。
中学生も、毎日の行動で海の未来を変えることができる。
海の問題は国や企業だけが解決できる。
魚は食べないほうがよい。
questions.answer: 中学生も、毎日の行動で海の未来を変えることができる。

choice_notes.プラスチックはすべて使うのをやめるべきだ。: そこまでは言っていない。
choice_notes.海の問題は国や企業だけが解決できる。: 第5段落で中学生にもできることを述べている。

questions.explanation: 第5段落で「中学生に何ができるか」を問い、最後に「毎日の行動が海の未来を変えられる」とまとめている。

questions.question: はじめの壁のようすについて、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: 町役場の中にあった。
美しい絵が描かれていた。
駅の隣にあり、通る人はだれも見なかった。
新しく建てられたばかりだった。
questions.answer: 駅の隣にあり、通る人はだれも見なかった。

choice_notes.美しい絵が描かれていた。: 1-2 で落書きでおおわれていた。

questions.explanation: 1-1 an old gray wall standing next to the station、1-3 People walking past the wall never looked at it.

questions.question: What did Yuto need before he painted the wall?
choices: Help from a famous artist.
Agreement from the people living near the wall.
Mr. Ono's bookstore.
Money from the town office.
questions.answer: Agreement from the people living near the wall.
questions.explanation: 2-4 "You can do it if the people living near the wall say yes."

questions.question: 下線部（1）で小野さんが言いたいこととして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 壁は町の歴史そのものだ。
壁はこわしたほうがよい。
壁はただの壁で、絵を描く必要はない。
壁は自分の本屋のものだ。
questions.answer: 壁はただの壁で、絵を描く必要はない。

choice_notes.壁はただの壁で、絵を描く必要はない。: 直後の「絵を描くなんて時間のむだだ」に合う。
choice_notes.壁は町の歴史そのものだ。: このときは反対している。

questions.explanation: 3-3 の後半 Painting it is a waste of time. から、絵を描くことに反対している。

questions.question: 小野さんに反対されたときの悠斗について、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: 計画をやめることにした。
町役場に、小野さんを説得するよう頼んだ。
あきらめずに何度も本屋へ行き、自分の絵を見せた。
別の壁を探しに行った。
questions.answer: あきらめずに何度も本屋へ行き、自分の絵を見せた。
questions.explanation: 3-4 he did not give up. 3-5 He went to the bookstore again and again and showed Mr. Ono his drawings.

questions.question: 小野さんの気持ちが変わったきっかけとして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 町役場の人に説得された。
悠斗の両親に頼まれた。
壁の絵でお金がもらえると聞いた。
100年前の駅の絵を見て、そこで働いていた父のことを思い出した。
questions.answer: 100年前の駅の絵を見て、そこで働いていた父のことを思い出した。
questions.explanation: 100年前の駅の絵を長い間見つめ、「父はこの駅で働いていた」と話し、写真を渡している。

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入る最も適切な語句を選びなさい。
choices: to wear a black hat
worn a black hat
wearing a black hat
wore a black hat
questions.answer: wearing a black hat

choice_notes.wore a black hat: 動詞の過去形は、名詞を後ろから説明できない。
choice_notes.wearing a black hat: 「黒い帽子をかぶった（かぶっている）男」。現在分詞が後ろから説明する。
choice_notes.worn a black hat: 過去分詞では「かぶられた」になる。
choice_notes.to wear a black hat: 「かぶるための男」では意味が通らない。

questions.explanation: 4-5 the man wearing a black hat と同じ形。現在分詞＋語句が名詞を後ろから説明する。

questions.question: この話の題名として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: How to Paint a Picture
A Wall That Brought a Town Together
A Bookstore by the Station
The History of Graffiti
questions.answer: A Wall That Brought a Town Together

choice_notes.How to Paint a Picture: 絵の描き方の話ではない。
choice_notes.A Wall That Brought a Town Together: 町の人がいっしょに壁に絵を描いた話。
choice_notes.The History of Graffiti: 落書きの歴史の話ではない。

questions.explanation: 反対していた小野さんもふくめ、町の人がいっしょに壁に町の歴史を描いた話。

questions.question: 学校が考えている新しいきまりとして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 制服を新しいデザインにする。
金曜日を休みにする。
生徒が自分の服を着てもよいことにする。
制服の値段を下げる。
questions.answer: 生徒が自分の服を着てもよいことにする。
questions.explanation: 1-2 Our school is thinking about a new rule: students can wear their own clothes.

questions.question: Why does Mei think uniforms save time?
choices: Because she doesn't have to think about what she should wear.
Because the school is near her house.
Because she can sleep in her uniform.
Because uniforms are cheap.
questions.answer: Because she doesn't have to think about what she should wear.

値段の話は時間の理由ではない。

questions.explanation: 2-2 I don't have to think about what I should wear. 2-3 That saves a lot of time.

questions.question: 卓也の意見として本文の内容に合うものを、2つ選びなさい。
choices: 冬の制服は3万円より高い。
制服は家族の助けになる。
制服は暑い日には着心地がよくない。
自分の服はお金がかかりすぎる。
金曜日も制服を着るべきだ。
questions.answer: 冬の制服は3万円より高い。 ／ 制服は暑い日には着心地がよくない。

choice_notes.自分の服はお金がかかりすぎる。: 芽衣やサラが言っていること。

questions.explanation: 3-3 A winter uniform costs more than 30,000 yen. 3-4 they are not comfortable on hot days.

questions.question: 下線部（1）の意味として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 服は、値段の高さを表す。
服は、学校の名前を表す。
服は、家族のことを表す。
服は、その人らしさを表す。
questions.answer: 服は、その人らしさを表す。

choice_notes.服は、その人らしさを表す。: who I am は「私がどんな人か」。

questions.explanation: who I am は間接疑問で「私がだれか（どんな人か）」。服が自分らしさを表すので、選ぶのが楽しい。

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入る最も適切な語句を選びなさい。
choices: to buy
bought
buy
buying
questions.answer: to buy

choice_notes.buying: feel pressure buying とは言わない。
choice_notes.to buy: 「～しなければというプレッシャー」。名詞 pressure を不定詞が後ろから説明する。
choice_notes.buy: 原形だけでは入らない。

questions.explanation: pressure to buy ~ で「～を買わなければというプレッシャー」（不定詞の形容詞的用法）。

questions.question: 卓也の新しい提案として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 毎日、自分の服を着る。
制服をやめる。
金曜日を休みにする。
ふだんは制服で、金曜日は自分の服を選べるようにする。
questions.answer: ふだんは制服で、金曜日は自分の服を選べるようにする。
questions.explanation: 7-2 We wear uniforms on most days, but we can choose our own clothes on Fridays.

questions.question: 加藤先生がこの後することとして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 今日の生徒の意見を校長先生に伝える。
その場で新しいきまりを決める。
新しい制服を注文する。
カナダの学校に連絡する。
questions.answer: 今日の生徒の意見を校長先生に伝える。
questions.explanation: 10-2 I'll tell the principal what you said today.（what you said ＝あなたたちが言ったこと）

questions.question: 「食品ロス」の説明として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 動物のえさにするための食べ物
まだ食べられるのに捨てられる食べ物
外国から輸入した食べ物
店で売れ残った野菜だけ
questions.answer: まだ食べられるのに捨てられる食べ物
questions.explanation: 1-2 Food that can still be eaten but is thrown away is called "food loss."

questions.question: 日本の食品ロスについて、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: すべて店から出ている。
家庭から出るのは1割ほどだ。
約半分が家庭から出ている。
毎年100万トン出ている。
questions.answer: 約半分が家庭から出ている。
questions.explanation: 1-4 About half of it comes from homes.

questions.question: グラフから、「食べる前に悪くなった」を選んだ家庭の割合を選びなさい。

choice_notes.10%: 10% は「賞味期限が過ぎていた」。
choice_notes.40%: グラフのいちばん長い棒。3-1 の the most common reason。

questions.explanation: グラフの1行目 Food went bad before we ate it が 40%。

questions.question: グラフで、2番目に多い理由を選びなさい。
choices: Other
We bought too much.
We cooked too much.
The best-before date was over.
questions.answer: We cooked too much.
questions.explanation: 3-3 The second reason was "We cooked too much."

questions.question: What should we do before shopping?
choices: Cook a lot of food.
Buy many vegetables.
Throw away old food.
Check what we have in the fridge.
questions.answer: Check what we have in the fridge.

4-4 では「ちょうどよい量を作る」。

questions.explanation: 4-2 First, check what you have in the fridge before shopping.

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入る最も適切な語を選びなさい。
choices: what
that
where
who
questions.answer: that

choice_notes.who: 先行詞 the food は人ではない。
choice_notes.what: what は先行詞をふくむので、the food の後には使わない。
choice_notes.that: 先行詞 the food を説明する目的格の関係代名詞（省略もできる）。
choice_notes.where: 場所を表す語ではない。

questions.explanation: the food that you need で「あなたが必要な食べ物」。that は need の目的語の働きをする。

questions.question: この発表で最も伝えたいことを選びなさい。
choices: 食品ロスは店だけの問題だ。
冷蔵庫は大きいほうがよい。
それぞれの家庭の行動で、市の食品ロスを減らすことができる。
野菜や果物は買わないほうがよい。
questions.answer: それぞれの家庭の行動で、市の食品ロスを減らすことができる。
questions.explanation: 4-5 If each family does these things, we can make our city's food loss much smaller.

questions.question: ミツバチについて、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: コロニーには女王バチがたくさんいる。
働きバチは、ふだんは巣から出ない。
働きバチは、花を探すために毎日巣から飛び立つ。
ミツバチは夜に花を探す。
questions.answer: 働きバチは、花を探すために毎日巣から飛び立つ。
questions.explanation: 1-3 The worker bees fly out of the hive every day to look for flowers.

questions.question: カール・フォン・フリッシュについて、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: ハチが情報を伝えるためにおどることを発見し、ノーベル賞を受けた。
約9年前にハチの研究を始めた。
アメリカの科学者だった。
ハチの巣の作り方を研究した。
questions.answer: ハチが情報を伝えるためにおどることを発見し、ノーベル賞を受けた。

choice_notes.ハチの巣の作り方を研究した。: 研究したのは情報の伝え方。

questions.explanation: 2-3 He found that bees "dance" to share information. 2-4 For this discovery, he won the Nobel Prize in 1973.

questions.question: What do the other bees do after they see a round dance?
choices: They build a new hive.
They look for flowers far away.
They go to sleep in the hive.
They fly out and look for flowers near the hive.
questions.answer: They fly out and look for flowers near the hive.
questions.explanation: 3-3 This dance makes the other bees fly out and look for flowers near the hive.（make + 人 + 原形）

questions.question:
本文には次の英文が抜けています。入る場所として最も適切なものを、本文中の【A】〜【D】から選びなさい。
For example, if the bee runs straight up, the flowers are in the direction of the sun.
choices: A
B
C
D
questions.answer: B

choice_notes.A: まだ8の字ダンスの説明が始まったところで、「方向」の話が出ていない。
choice_notes.B: 直前の「まっすぐ進む向きは花の方向を表す」の具体例になる。
choice_notes.C: 直前は距離の話なので、方向の例はつながらない。
choice_notes.D: 新しいすみかを選ぶ話の途中で、つながらない。

questions.explanation: For example の文は「向き＝方向」の例なので、4-2 の直後の【B】に入る。

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入るように、語句を並べかえなさい。
questions.prompt_ja: 語句を並べかえなさい（1つ不要な語句があります）
questions.answer: where the flowers are
questions.explanation: 間接疑問「花がどこにあるか」は 疑問詞 where + 主語 the flowers + 動詞 are の語順。主語が複数なので is は使わない。lets the other bees know ~ は let + 人 + 原形。

questions.question: 本文の内容に合うものを2つ選びなさい。
choices: 円形ダンスは、花が遠くにあることを表す。
ダンスが長いと、花は遠くにある。
まっすぐ進む向きは、花までの距離を表す。
ハチは、新しいすみかを選ぶのにも同じダンスを使う。
ハチはことばを使って話し合う。
questions.answer: ダンスが長いと、花は遠くにある。 ／ ハチは、新しいすみかを選ぶのにも同じダンスを使う。

choice_notes.まっすぐ進む向きは、花までの距離を表す。: 4-2 で向きは方向、4-3 で長さが距離。

questions.explanation: 4-4 A long dance means that the flowers are far away. 5-1 ... bees use the same dance to choose a new home.

questions.question: 筆者がこの文章で最も伝えたいことを選びなさい。
choices: ノーベル賞をとるには長い研究が必要だ。
ハチは人間にとって危険な生き物だ。
ハチは花のみつだけを集める。
ハチはことばがなくても、ダンスでうまく協力している。
questions.answer: ハチはことばがなくても、ダンスでうまく協力している。
questions.explanation: 5-3 Bees do not have words, but they work together very well.

questions.question: けがをする前の遥について、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: 足が遅いのでリレーに出られなかった。
クラスでいちばん足が速く、リレーのアンカーに選ばれた。
運動会に出たくないと思っていた。
リレーのコーチをしていた。
questions.answer: クラスでいちばん足が速く、リレーのアンカーに選ばれた。

choice_notes.リレーのコーチをしていた。: コーチになったのはけがの後。

questions.explanation: 1-1 Haruka was the fastest runner in her class. 1-2 She was chosen as the anchor ...

questions.question: What happened to Haruka two weeks before sports day?
choices: She lost the baton.
She caught a bad cold.
She fell down the stairs and broke her leg.
She moved to another school.
questions.answer: She fell down the stairs and broke her leg.
questions.explanation: 2-1 Haruka fell down the stairs at the station and broke her leg.

questions.question: 下線部（1）で遥が表している気持ちとして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 今すぐ学校へ行きたいのに、行けなくてつらい。
学校には行きたくない。
空を飛ぶ練習をしたい。
鳥を飼いたい。
questions.answer: 今すぐ学校へ行きたいのに、行けなくてつらい。

choice_notes.空を飛ぶ練習をしたい。: 本当に飛びたいわけではない。
choice_notes.今すぐ学校へ行きたいのに、行けなくてつらい。: 仮定法で「本当はできない」ことを表している。

questions.explanation: If I were ~, I could ... は事実と反対の仮定（仮定法）。足を折って行けないので「鳥なら飛んでいけるのに」と言っている。

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入る最も適切な語句を選びなさい。
choices: could
am able
will
can
questions.answer: could

choice_notes.can: I wish の後は過去形にする。
choice_notes.could: I wish I could ~ で「～できればいいのに」。
choice_notes.will: I wish の後には will は使わない。
choice_notes.am able: be able to の形になっていない。

questions.explanation: I wish + 主語 + 過去形（could）で、実現できない願いを表す。

questions.question: 森先生の提案と遥の返事について、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: 運動会を休むようにすすめ、遥は断った。
チームのコーチになるようにすすめたが、遥は断った。
アンカーを続けるようにすすめ、遥は断った。
チームのコーチになるようにすすめ、遥は引き受けた。
questions.answer: チームのコーチになるようにすすめ、遥は引き受けた。

choice_notes.アンカーを続けるようにすすめ、遥は断った。: 走れないので本文と合わない。

questions.explanation: 3-3 Will you be the coach of your team? 3-4 Haruka thought for a while and said yes.

questions.question: 遥が健太にしたアドバイスとして、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 結衣がテープの線に来たら、走り出すこと。
もっとゆっくり走ること。
バトンを受け取ってから走り出すこと。
後ろを見ながら走ること。
questions.answer: 結衣がテープの線に来たら、走り出すこと。

choice_notes.バトンを受け取ってから走り出すこと。: スピードを落とすのが問題だった。

questions.explanation: 4-3 で健太がバトンの前にスピードを落とすことに気づき、4-4 で「結衣がこの線に来たら走り出して」と言った。

questions.question: 下線部（2）の意味として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: 足が治って、また走れるようになった。
鳥が嫌いになった。
飛行機で学校に行けるようになった。
コーチとしてチームの役に立てたので、もう「鳥だったら」と思わなくなった。
questions.answer: コーチとしてチームの役に立てたので、もう「鳥だったら」と思わなくなった。

choice_notes.足が治って、また走れるようになった。: 2か月走れないので合わない。
choice_notes.コーチとしてチームの役に立てたので、もう「鳥だったら」と思わなくなった。: 5-3・5-4 と、2-4 の仮定法の言葉に合う。

questions.explanation: 2-4 では「鳥なら学校へ飛んでいけるのに」と嘆いていたが、コーチとしてチームを勝たせ「このメダルはコーチのものでもある」と言われた。もう翼（鳥になること）は必要なかった。

questions.question: 京都での自由時間について、本文の内容に合うものを選びなさい。
choices: 自由時間はない。
自由時間は4時間ある。
自由時間は2時間だ。
自由時間は1日中ある。
questions.answer: 自由時間は4時間ある。
questions.explanation: 1-1 We have four hours of free time in Kyoto, don't we?（付加疑問「～だよね」）

questions.question: 本文の（ ア ）に入る最も適切な語句を選びなさい。
choices: aren't they
isn't it
doesn't it
is it
questions.answer: isn't it

choice_notes.doesn't it: be動詞の文なので does は使わない。
choice_notes.is it: 肯定文の付加疑問は否定形。
choice_notes.isn't it: it's（it is）の肯定文なので、付加疑問は isn't it。

questions.explanation: 肯定文 it's far ... の付加疑問は「否定の短縮形 + 主語の代名詞」で isn't it?

questions.question: How long does it take to go to Kinkakuji by bus?
choices: About an hour and a half.
About fifteen minutes.
About forty minutes.
About four hours.
questions.answer: About forty minutes.
questions.explanation: 4-1 It takes about forty minutes by bus.

questions.question: 蓮の提案とその理由として、最も適切なものを選びなさい。
choices: バスが混むので、金閣寺には行かない。
夕方は人が少ないので、最後に金閣寺へ行く。
朝は人が少ないので、最初に金閣寺へ行く。
歩いて行けるので、バスは使わない。
questions.answer: 朝は人が少ないので、最初に金閣寺へ行く。

choice_notes.バスが混むので、金閣寺には行かない。: 行かないとは言っていない。

questions.explanation: 5-1 Then how about going there first? 5-2 In the morning, there are fewer people.

questions.question: 茶道の体験について、本文の内容に合うものを2つ選びなさい。
choices: お茶屋は金閣寺の近くにある。
料金は無料だ。
予約が必要だ。
エミリーはもう予約をした。
ホテルの中で体験できる。
questions.answer: お茶屋は金閣寺の近くにある。 ／ 予約が必要だ。
questions.explanation: 6-3 there is a small tea house near Kinkakuji. 8-2 We need to make a reservation, though.

questions.question: Has Emily made a reservation yet?
choices: Yes, she did.
No, she hasn't.
Yes, she has.
No, she didn't.
questions.answer: No, she hasn't.

passages.title: School Lunch in Japan
passages.body:
In Japan, many junior high school students eat school lunch in their classrooms. They do not go to a cafeteria. Some students carry the food from the kitchen and serve it to their classmates. These students wear white coats and caps.

A school lunch usually has rice or bread, soup, a main dish, and milk. Nutritionists plan the menu every month. They think about our health and the seasons. In autumn, we often eat sweet potatoes and chestnuts.

After lunch, everyone cleans the classroom together. Last year, a student from Canada visited our school. She was very surprised at these things. "In my country, students never serve lunch to their friends," she said. But she enjoyed our lunch time very much.

passages.title: The Red Umbrella
passages.body:
Last Saturday, Mika went to the library in her town. It was sunny in the morning, but she took her red umbrella with her. Her grandmother gave it to her on her birthday.

Mika read books in the library for three hours. At four o'clock, she looked out of the window. Outside, the rain came down hard. Near the door, a little boy stood alone. He did not have an umbrella, and he was sad.

Mika thought about her grandmother. Then she gave her umbrella to the boy. "Here you are. Please use it," she said. The boy smiled and said, "Thank you!" Mika ran home in the rain.

The next week, a woman came to Mika's house with the red umbrella. She was the boy's mother. She had a box of cookies and a letter from the boy for Mika. The letter said, "You are my hero." Mika showed the letter to her grandmother, and they both smiled.

passages.title: The Town Festival
passages.body:
Hi, Ken. What are you reading?

I'm reading a poster for the Midori Town Festival. It's on Sunday, August 12. Do you know about it?

No. What do people do there?

They dance in the street, and they eat food from many shops. My father makes yakisoba at a shop every year. His yakisoba is very popular.

That's great! I want to try it. Can I go with you?

Sure. Let's meet at the station at ten. Oh, and the dance starts at two in the afternoon. You can wear a yukata. My mother has a nice one.

Really? But I can't wear a yukata by myself.

Don't worry. My mother can help you.

Thank you, Ken. I can't wait!

passages.title: Our Favorite Sports
passages.body:
I'm Yuki, and I'm in Class 1-B. Last month, I did a survey in my class. I asked thirty-five students about their favorite sports. Please look at the graph.

Twelve students like soccer. It is number one in our class. Basketball is number two, and eight students like it. I like basketball, too.

Only four students chose swimming. I was surprised at this result. Our school has a big pool, and we have swimming classes in July.

Six students like tennis, and five students like baseball. Many students in our class play soccer at lunch time. Maybe soccer is number one for that reason.

passages.title: Giant Pandas
passages.body:
Giant pandas live in the mountains of China. They are black and white, and many people love them. But there are only about 1,900 giant pandas in the wild.

Pandas eat bamboo almost all day. An adult panda eats about 12 to 38 kilograms of bamboo every day. They cannot get much energy from bamboo, so they move slowly and sleep a lot.

A baby panda is very small at first. It weighs only about 100 grams. That is like one small orange! Its mother holds it carefully when it sleeps.

In the past, the number of pandas went down because people cut down the forests. Now people in China are protecting the forests, and the number is slowly going up. If we protect their home, we will see pandas in the wild for a long time.

passages.title: A New Friend from Brazil
passages.body:
One morning in April, a new student came to our class. His name was Leo, and he was from Brazil. He said, "Hello. I'm Leo. I don't speak Japanese well, but I will try hard."

At lunch time, Leo was eating alone. I wanted to talk with him, but I was nervous because my English was not good. Then I remembered his words, "I will try hard." So I went to his desk and said, "Hi, Leo. I'm Sota. Do you like soccer?"

Leo smiled. "Yes! I love soccer. I played it every day in Brazil," he said. We talked about soccer players for a long time. Leo told me about some Portuguese words, and I told him about some Japanese words.

Now Leo and I are good friends. Next month, there is a soccer tournament in our city. We are going to play in it together. I'm sure we will have a great time.

昼休み、レオは一人で食べていました。私は彼と話したかったのですが、英語がうまくないので緊張していました。そのとき、彼の「がんばります」という言葉を思い出しました。そこで私は彼の机のところへ行き、「やあ、レオ。ぼくは颯太。サッカーは好き？」と言いました。

レオはにっこりしました。「うん！サッカーが大好き。ブラジルでは毎日やっていたよ」と彼は言いました。私たちは長い時間、サッカー選手について話しました。レオはポルトガル語の言葉をいくつか教えてくれて、私は日本語の言葉をいくつか教えました。

今では、レオと私は仲のよい友だちです。来月、市でサッカー大会があります。私たちはいっしょにその大会に出るつもりです。きっと、すばらしい時間になると思います。

passages.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
passages.body:
Do you sleep well every night? Many junior high school students go to bed late because they have a lot of things to do. But sleep is very important for your body and your brain.

While you are sleeping, your brain is busy. It sorts the new information from the day. Then it keeps the important information in your memory. So if you want to remember new English words, you should sleep well after you study them.

Sleep also helps your body. When you sleep, your body makes a special hormone. It is necessary for growing and for getting well.

How many hours should you sleep? Doctors say that teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep every night. But many students in Japan sleep only about seven hours. One reason is their smartphones. The light from a screen tells your brain, "It's still daytime!"

Here are some tips for good sleep. First, try to go to bed at the same time every day. Second, stop using your phone thirty minutes before bed. Sleeping well is the first step to studying well.

passages.title: The Piano Contest
passages.body:
Aya started playing the piano when she was five. She loved practicing every day after school. Last summer, her teacher said, "You should enter the city piano contest."

Aya was excited, but she was also worried. She was not good at playing in front of many people. For two months, she practiced for three hours every day. Her fingers hurt, but she did not stop practicing. Her mother said, "Take a break, Aya." But Aya wanted to play the song perfectly.

On the day of the contest, Aya's hands were shaking on the stage. She started to play, but she made a mistake in the first minute. Her mind went blank. Then she remembered her teacher's words: "Enjoy playing. Don't worry about mistakes." She took a deep breath and continued.

Aya did not win a prize. But after the contest, a little girl came to her and said, "Your music was beautiful. I want to play like you." The girl's mother said, "My daughter started piano lessons this year." Aya smiled, and she learned something important that day. Making mistakes is not a bad thing if you keep trying.

passages.title: Choosing a Club
passages.body:
Ms. Green, I can't decide on a club. Can you help me?

Of course. Which clubs are you thinking about?

The tennis club and the science club. I like sports, but I'm also interested in science.

Let's think about them together. The tennis club practices five days a week. The science club meets only twice a week.

So I can have more free time in the science club. I want to study hard, too.

That's true. But the tennis club is more popular. It has thirty members, and the science club has only eight. The members of the tennis club are very friendly, too.

Thirty! In a big club, I can't play in games very often, right?

Maybe not in your first year. In the science club, every member does an experiment every week. Last year, the club won a prize at the city science fair. They also visit a science museum together every summer.

That sounds exciting! I think the science club is better for me.

Good. You can also play tennis with your friends on weekends. Some science club members do that.

That's a great idea. Thank you, Ms. Green!

passages.title: How We Come to School
passages.body:
Our school newspaper team did a survey about the ways of getting to school. We asked 200 first-year students and 200 third-year students. Each student chose one way. The table shows the results.

Walking is the most popular way for first-year students. More than half of them walk to school. Many first-year students live near the school, so they do not need bikes. But for third-year students, the bike is more popular than walking.

Why do more third-year students ride bikes? We talked with some of them. One student said, "I go to a juku after school, so a bike is faster than walking." Another student said, "In some areas, first-year students are not allowed to ride bikes to school." We also think that third-year students are more careful on busy roads.

Not many students take a bus or a train. Most of them live in towns far from the school, and they usually leave home before seven o'clock. The bus is a little more popular than the train in both years. We hope this survey is useful for new students.

passages.title: The Art of Origami
passages.body:
Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper. You need only one square piece of paper. No scissors or glue are used.

Paper was brought to Japan from China about 1,400 years ago. At first, paper was very expensive, so origami was used only for special events. Later, paper became cheaper, and many children began to enjoy origami. In the Edo period, books about origami were also made.

Today, origami is loved by people all over the world. The paper crane is the most famous origami. In Japan, people often give a thousand paper cranes to sick friends. The cranes are a wish for good health. In many countries, people enjoy origami at schools and in clubs.

Origami is also used in science. For example, a large solar panel for a space satellite was folded like origami. It became small in the rocket and opened in space. This way of folding is called "Miura-ori." A Japanese scientist made it. Today, this idea is also used for maps.

Origami is more than a game for children. It connects art, culture, and science. Why don't you fold a paper crane today?

passages.translation:
折り紙は、紙を折る日本の芸術です。必要なのは正方形の紙1枚だけです。はさみやのりは使われません。

紙は約1,400年前に中国から日本に伝えられました。最初は紙がとても高価だったので、折り紙は特別な行事のためだけに使われました。のちに紙が安くなり、多くの子どもたちが折り紙を楽しむようになりました。江戸時代には、折り紙の本も作られました。

今日、折り紙は世界中の人々に愛されています。紙の鶴は、いちばん有名な折り紙です。日本では、病気の友だちに千羽鶴をおくることがよくあります。鶴は、健康を願う気持ちなのです。多くの国で、人々は学校やクラブで折り紙を楽しんでいます。

折り紙は科学にも使われています。たとえば、人工衛星の大きな太陽光パネルは、折り紙のように折りたたまれました。それはロケットの中では小さくなり、宇宙で開きました。この折り方は「ミウラ折り」と呼ばれています。日本の科学者が考え出しました。今日、この考え方は地図にも使われています。

折り紙は、子どもの遊び以上のものです。芸術、文化、そして科学をつないでいます。今日、紙の鶴を折ってみませんか。

passages.title: Grandpa's Garden
passages.body:
My grandfather has lived in a small village in Nagano for seventy years. He has a big vegetable garden behind his house. I have visited him every summer since I was a little child.

This summer, Grandpa was in the hospital because he hurt his leg. "Who will take care of my garden?" he said. I said, "I will!" But it was my first time growing vegetables.

Every morning, I got up at five and watered the tomatoes and cucumbers. It was hard work in the hot sun. One day, I found that some birds were eating the tomatoes. I called Grandpa at the hospital. He laughed and said, "Put a net over them. Birds love tomatoes as much as we do."

At the end of August, Grandpa came home. He looked at the garden and said, "You've done a great job." We ate the tomatoes together. I have never eaten such delicious tomatoes. Since then, I have become interested in farming. I have already decided to visit Grandpa again next summer.

passages.title: Welcome to Perth
passages.body:
Welcome to Perth, Hana! How was your flight?

It was long, but I'm fine. I've wanted to come to Australia for a long time.

I'm glad to hear that. Have you ever been abroad before?

No, this is my first time. I've studied English for six years, but I've never talked with people in English outside class. I'm a little nervous. At school, we usually read and write English, and we don't speak it much.

Don't worry. You can practice with us every day. This is our son, Sam. He's eleven. We love meeting students from other countries. Last year, a boy from France stayed with us for a month.

Hi, Hana! Have you seen a kangaroo yet?

Not yet. I've only seen them on TV.

There's a big park near our house. Many kangaroos live there. Let's go tomorrow morning! You can also see many beautiful birds there.

Sam, Hana has just arrived. She needs some rest.

It's OK. I'd love to go! I'll go to bed early tonight. Sam, can you teach me some Australian English, too?

Of course he can. Now let's go home and have dinner.

passages.title: Reading Time Changed Our School
passages.body:
I'm Daiki, a member of the library committee. Since April, our committee has made a report about the library every month. The table shows the number of books for each grade. We wanted to know about students' reading.

In April and May, students did not borrow many books. Third-year students borrowed the fewest books. They have been very busy with club activities and studying for exams. First-year students borrowed the most books in both months.

In June, we started a morning reading time. Every student reads a book for ten minutes before classes. Since then, the number of books has gone up in every grade. The number for third-year students has almost doubled. Many teachers have joined the reading time, too.

Some students have told us, "I've found a new favorite writer." We hope more students will enjoy reading. In September, we are going to show our favorite books on a board in the library. If you have a good book, please tell us about it. Let's make our library a more exciting place together!

passages.title: Plastic in the Ocean
passages.body:
Look at the things around you. How many of them are made of plastic? Plastic is a material that is cheap, light, and strong. Because of these good points, people all over the world use it every day. But plastic has also caused a serious problem in the ocean. This problem is getting bigger every year.

Every year, about eight million tons of plastic waste goes into the sea. Most of it comes from land. For example, a plastic bag that someone drops on the street is often carried to a river by the wind and rain. Then the river takes it to the sea.

Plastic does not disappear easily. In the sea, it is broken into very small pieces by the sun and the waves. Pieces that are smaller than five millimeters are called microplastics. Fish and birds often eat them because they look like food. Scientists have found microplastics even in the deep sea and in Arctic ice. Some of the plastic that fish eat may come back to us when we eat fish.

Some people say that the plastic in the sea will be heavier than all the fish in the sea by 2050. That is a shocking idea. Many countries and companies have started to take action. For example, some countries have stopped giving plastic bags to shoppers for free. In Japan, people have paid for plastic bags at stores since 2020.

What can we do as junior high school students? We can carry our own bags and bottles. We can also join beach clean-up events that are held in many towns. One plastic bottle may not look important, but the actions we take every day can change the future of the ocean.

passages.translation:
身の回りのものを見てください。そのうちいくつがプラスチックでできているでしょうか。プラスチックは、安くて軽くて丈夫な素材です。こうした長所があるので、世界中の人々が毎日それを使っています。しかしプラスチックは、海で深刻な問題も引き起こしてきました。この問題は、年々大きくなっています。

毎年、約800万トンのプラスチックごみが海に流れこみます。そのほとんどは陸から来ます。たとえば、だれかが道に落としたビニール袋は、風や雨によって川へ運ばれることがよくあります。そして、川がそれを海へ運びます。

プラスチックは簡単にはなくなりません。海の中では、日光や波によって、とても小さなかけらに砕かれます。5ミリメートルより小さいかけらは、マイクロプラスチックと呼ばれます。魚や鳥は、それらがえさのように見えるので、よく食べてしまいます。科学者は、深海や北極の氷の中からさえ、マイクロプラスチックを見つけています。魚が食べたプラスチックの一部は、私たちが魚を食べるときに、私たちのところへもどってくるかもしれません。

2050年までに、海のプラスチックは海にいるすべての魚より重くなるだろうと言う人もいます。それは衝撃的な考えです。多くの国や企業が、行動を起こし始めています。たとえば、買い物客にビニール袋を無料で渡すのをやめた国もあります。日本では、2020年から店のビニール袋にお金を払っています。

私たち中学生に何ができるでしょうか。自分の袋や水筒を持ち歩くことができます。多くの町で行われている海岸の清掃活動に参加することもできます。ペットボトル1本は大切に見えないかもしれませんが、私たちが毎日とる行動が、海の未来を変えることができるのです。

passages.title: The Painted Wall
passages.body:
There was an old gray wall standing next to the station in Yuto's town. It was covered with graffiti written by someone at night. People walking past the wall never looked at it. "This wall makes our town dark," Yuto thought. Yuto loved painting more than anything.

One day, Yuto went to the town office with a plan. "Can we paint a picture on the wall? I want to paint our town's history on it," he said. The man working at the office liked the idea. "You can do it if the people living near the wall say yes," he said.

Yuto visited the houses and shops near the station and talked with the people. Most of them agreed, but Mr. Ono, an old man running a small bookstore, did not. "A wall is a wall," he said. "Painting it is a waste of time." Yuto was disappointed, but he did not give up. He went to the bookstore again and again and showed Mr. Ono his drawings.

One of the drawings showed the station a hundred years ago. Mr. Ono looked at it for a long time. "My father worked at this station," he said quietly. He took out an old photo. "He is the man wearing a black hat in this photo." "Use this," he said, and gave it to Yuto.

During the summer vacation, Yuto and more than thirty people, including Mr. Ono, painted the wall together. The finished wall shows the town's history, from the old station to the festival held every autumn. Now people walking past it often stop and take pictures. Mr. Ono sometimes stands in front of the man wearing a black hat and smiles.

passages.title: School Uniforms or Our Own Clothes?
passages.body:
Today's topic is school uniforms. Our school is thinking about a new rule: students can wear their own clothes. I'd like to know what you think. Mei, can you tell us your opinion first?

I think we should keep uniforms. In the morning, I don't have to think about what I should wear. That saves a lot of time. Also, uniforms are good for our families because they don't have to buy a lot of clothes. I also like our uniform because it shows that we belong to the same school.

I don't agree. Uniforms are expensive. A winter uniform costs more than 30,000 yen. And they are not comfortable on hot days. I wonder why we must wear jackets on hot days in May. Many students in my class feel the same way.

In my school in Canada, we don't have uniforms. Everyone wears clothes they like. I enjoy choosing my clothes because they show who I am. On cold days, we can wear warm clothes, and on hot days, we can wear T-shirts.

But some students may worry about how they look. They may feel pressure to buy fashionable clothes.

That's a good point. Actually, some of my friends in Canada spend a lot of money on clothes. So I understand what you mean, Mei.

Then how about this idea? We wear uniforms on most days, but we can choose our own clothes on Fridays. Then we can enjoy our own style, and we can still keep the good points of uniforms.

Interesting. Do you know if other schools have tried something like that?

Yes. My cousin's school started "Free Clothes Friday" last year. He says students look forward to Fridays now. Some students also say that they talk more with their classmates about clothes and music.

Thank you, everyone. I'll tell the principal what you said today. Let's talk about this topic again next week.

passages.title: Food Loss in Our City
passages.body:
Do you know how much food is thrown away in Japan? Food that can still be eaten but is thrown away is called "food loss." Japan produces more than four million tons of food loss every year. About half of it comes from homes. The total is about one bowl of rice per person every day.

Our group did a survey of 120 families who live in our city. We asked them about the main reason for throwing away food. The graph shows the results. Each family chose one reason.

The most common reason was "Food went bad before we ate it." Many people buy vegetables and fruit that they cannot finish. The second reason was "We cooked too much." Ten percent of the families chose "The best-before date was over." Some of them said, "We didn't notice the date because the food was at the back of the fridge." Other families said that they often forget about food in the freezer, too.

We think that there are three things everyone can do. First, check what you have in the fridge before shopping. Second, buy only the food that you need. Third, cook the right amount, and use leftovers for the next meal. If each family does these things, we can make our city's food loss much smaller.

We also asked the families about the things that they are already doing. Many families write the dates on food and put it at the front of the fridge. One family said, "We have a 'leftover day' every Sunday. On that day, we cook only with food that is left in the fridge." We think these ideas are easy and fun. Why don't you try one of them at home this week?

日本でどれくらいの食べ物が捨てられているか、知っていますか。まだ食べられるのに捨てられる食べ物は「食品ロス」と呼ばれます。日本では、毎年400万トン以上の食品ロスが出ています。その約半分は家庭から出ています。全体では、一人あたり毎日ご飯茶わん1杯ほどになります。

私たちの班は、市に住む120の家庭を調査しました。食べ物を捨てるいちばんの理由をたずねました。グラフはその結果です。各家庭が一つの理由を選びました。

いちばん多かった理由は「食べる前に悪くなった」でした。多くの人は、食べきれない野菜や果物を買ってしまいます。2番目の理由は「作りすぎた」でした。10パーセントの家庭が「賞味期限が過ぎていた」を選びました。「食べ物が冷蔵庫の奥にあったので、日付に気づかなかった」と言った家庭もありました。冷凍庫の食べ物のこともよく忘れてしまう、と言った家庭もありました。

私たちは、だれにでもできることが3つあると考えます。まず、買い物の前に、冷蔵庫に何があるかを確かめること。次に、必要な食べ物だけを買うこと。3つ目に、ちょうどよい量を作り、残り物を次の食事に使うことです。それぞれの家庭がこうしたことをすれば、市の食品ロスをずっと少なくできます。

私たちは、各家庭がすでにしていることについてもたずねました。多くの家庭が、食べ物に日付を書いて冷蔵庫の手前に置いています。ある家庭は「毎週日曜日を『残り物の日』にしています。その日は、冷蔵庫に残っている食べ物だけで料理をします」と言いました。これらの考えは簡単で楽しいと私たちは思います。今週、家でどれか一つを試してみませんか。

passages.title: How Honeybees Talk
passages.body:
Honeybees live in large groups called colonies. A colony has one queen bee and thousands of worker bees. The worker bees fly out of the hive every day to look for flowers. They collect nectar and pollen from the flowers and bring them back to the hive. But how do the bees tell other bees where the flowers are?

About ninety years ago, an Austrian scientist named Karl von Frisch studied this question. He watched bees closely for many years. He found that bees "dance" to share information. For this discovery, he won the Nobel Prize in 1973. His work helped other scientists study insects in new ways.

When the flowers are near the hive, a bee does a "round dance." It moves in small circles again and again. This dance makes the other bees fly out and look for flowers near the hive. When the flowers are far away, the bee does a "waggle dance." It runs in a straight line while it shakes its body, and then it turns and comes back.

The waggle dance tells the bees two things. The direction of the straight line shows the direction of the flowers. The length of the dance shows the distance. A long dance means that the flowers are far away. In this way, the dancer lets the other bees know where the flowers are.

Scientists have also seen bees use the same dance to choose a new home. Many bees dance for different places, and finally the group decides on the best one. Bees do not have words, but they work together very well. Their dance helps us understand that communication is more than words. Next time you see a bee near a flower, watch it carefully. Maybe it is getting ready for its next dance!

passages.title: The Coach in a Wheelchair
passages.body:
Haruka was the fastest runner in her class. She was chosen as the anchor of the class relay team for sports day. Every day after school, she practiced passing the baton with her teammates. "We're going to win this year," she always said.

But two weeks before sports day, Haruka fell down the stairs at the station and broke her leg. The doctor said, "You can't run for two months." At home, she looked out of the window and saw some birds flying in the sky. "If I were a bird, I could fly to school right now," she said. "I wish I could run with my team."

The next day, her teacher, Ms. Mori, visited her. "Your team needs you, Haruka," she said. "You can't run, but you know a lot about running. Will you be the coach of your team?" Haruka thought for a while and said yes. "Thank you, Ms. Mori. I'll do my best," she said.

From the next week, Haruka went to school in a wheelchair. She watched her teammates practice and gave them advice. She noticed that Kenta, the new anchor, always slowed down before he took the baton. "Start running when Yui reaches this line," she told him, and she put a line of white tape on the ground. Little by little, the team's baton passing became smoother. Haruka was happy because she could help her team again.

On sports day, Haruka watched the relay from her wheelchair. Her team passed the baton perfectly and finished first. The members ran to Haruka and put the gold medal around her neck. "This medal is yours, too, Coach," Kenta said. Haruka smiled. She didn't need wings anymore.

passages.title: Free Time in Kyoto
passages.body:
We have four hours of free time in Kyoto, don't we? Let's decide where to go.

I want to visit Kinkakuji. It's very famous, isn't it?

Yes! I've seen pictures of it in a book. How beautiful it is! But it's far from our hotel, isn't it?

It takes about forty minutes by bus. The buses are often crowded, so it may take longer. Let's check the bus times on the internet before we go.

Then how about going there first? In the morning, there are fewer people.

Good idea. After that, I'd like to try a tea ceremony. My host mother told me that there is a small tea house near Kinkakuji.

That sounds nice. How much is it?

It's 1,500 yen. We need to make a reservation, though.

Haven't you made one yet?

No, I haven't. I'll call them tonight.

Your plan looks good. But don't forget the rule. You must come back to the hotel by one o'clock.

We will, Mr. Hayashi. Kyoto will be fun, won't it?

I'm sure it will. And take a lot of pictures for the school newspaper.

By the way, where are we going to have lunch?

I'd like to eat Kyoto-style tofu. My host father says it is very soft and delicious.

There is a tofu restaurant on the way back to the hotel. My brother went there last year, and he said that it wasn't expensive.

Perfect! Then our plan is Kinkakuji first, then the tea ceremony, and then lunch at the tofu restaurant. We'll also have time for buying souvenirs, won't we?

I think so. What a busy day it'll be! But I'm sure we'll have a great time. I can't wait for the trip!

ぼくは金閣寺に行きたいな。とても有名だよね。

バスで約40分かかるよ。バスはよく混むから、もっとかかるかも。出かける前に、インターネットでバスの時間を調べよう。

じゃあ、最初にそこへ行くのはどう？朝は人が少ないよ。

いい考え。その後、茶道を体験したいな。ホストマザーが、金閣寺の近くに小さなお茶屋さんがあるって教えてくれたの。

いいね。いくらかかるの？

1,500円よ。でも、予約が必要なの。

まだ予約してないの？

うん、まだなの。今夜、電話するね。

いい計画ですね。でも、きまりを忘れないでください。1時までにホテルにもどらなければいけません。

わかりました、林先生。京都、楽しみですね。

きっと楽しいですよ。それと、学校新聞のために写真をたくさん撮ってきてください。

ところで、お昼はどこで食べる？

京都風の豆腐料理を食べたいな。ホストファーザーが、とてもやわらかくておいしいって言うの。

ホテルへの帰り道に、豆腐料理の店があるよ。兄が去年行って、高くなかったって言ってた。

完ぺき！じゃあ計画は、まず金閣寺、次に茶道、それから豆腐料理の店でお昼だね。おみやげを買う時間もあるよね。

あると思う。なんて忙しい日になるんだろう！でも、きっとすごく楽しいよ。旅行が待ちきれないな！

passages.title: Tourists in Our Town
passages.body:
I live in Kawase, a small town famous for its hot springs. For my social studies project, I looked into the number of tourists who visit our town. The table shows the numbers from 2019 to 2025.

In 2021, the number of tourists went down a lot because people could not travel freely. Since then, the number of Japanese visitors has come back. In 2025, it was almost the same as in 2019.

The number of visitors from abroad has grown even faster. In 2025, about 21,000 people came from abroad. Many of them come from Taiwan, Korea, and Australia. They enjoy the hot springs and the snow in winter.

But there is a problem. Most signs and menus in our town are written only in Japanese. Last month, I saw a family from Australia standing in front of a map at the station. They looked confused. I wanted to help them, but I was shy, and I couldn't speak to them. "If I were braver, I could help them," I thought.

I wish our town had more signs in English. So I'm going to make an English map of our town with my classmates. We will put it at the station and at the hot springs. I also want to practice English, so I can talk to visitors next time.

Last week, I talked about my plan with Mr. Sato, a man who works at the town office. "Your map will help many visitors enjoy our town," he said. He also told me that the town is going to make new signs in English next year. I was very happy to hear that. I hope that more people from abroad will visit Kawase and love it as much as I do.

passages.title: The Long History of the Bicycle
passages.body:
Today, the bicycle is one of the most common ways of getting around. There are about one billion bicycles in the world. But do you know how the bicycle was born?

In 1817, a German man named Karl Drais made a strange machine. It had two wheels, but it had no pedals. People sat on it and pushed the ground with their feet. Drais made this machine because many horses had died after a very cold summer, and people needed a new way of traveling.

About fifty years later, people in France put pedals on the front wheel. To go faster, makers started to build bicycles with a very large front wheel. Some front wheels were taller than a man. These bicycles were fast, but they were also dangerous. Many riders fell and got hurt. Because of their strange shape, people called them "penny-farthings."

In 1885, an English inventor made the "safety bicycle." It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that moved the back wheel. Riders could put their feet on the ground easily, so it was much safer. A few years later, tires filled with air were added, and riding became more comfortable. Our bicycles today look almost the same as the safety bicycle.

The bicycle also changed people's lives. Before bicycles became popular, many people had never traveled far from their villages. With bicycles, they could visit other towns and meet new people. A writer at that time said that the bicycle had given women more freedom than anything else. Even now, the bicycle is a simple machine that keeps changing the world. Today, many cities are building bike lanes because bicycles are good for the environment and for our health.

passages.title: Why Do We Forget?
passages.body:
Have you ever studied hard for a test and then forgotten almost everything a week later? If so, you are not alone. Forgetting is a natural part of how our brains work.

In the 1880s, a German scientist named Hermann Ebbinghaus did a famous experiment on memory. He made a list of meaningless "words" such as "ZOF" and "BIK," and tried to remember them. Then he checked how much he could still remember after different lengths of time. The results surprised many people. Only twenty minutes after learning, he had already forgotten about forty percent of the words. One day later, about seventy percent was gone. His results, shown as a curve on a graph, are now called "the forgetting curve."

Why does our brain forget so quickly? Scientists think that forgetting is actually useful. Every day, we see and hear a huge amount of information. If we remembered all of it, our brains would be too full to work well. So the brain keeps only the information that seems important and throws away the rest. This is why we can remember our friends' names but not what we ate for lunch a month ago.

Then how does the brain decide what is important? One important sign is repetition. When we meet the same information again and again, the brain thinks, "I need this," and keeps it for a longer time. Ebbinghaus found that each review made the forgetting curve less steep. In other words, we forget more slowly after every review.

This idea led to a study method called "spaced repetition." Instead of studying the same words ten times in one night, you review them after one day, then after three days, then after a week, and so on. Each time, you review them just before you are about to forget them. Many studies have shown that this method works much better than studying everything at once. In fact, some learning apps use it to decide which words you should review each day. For example, an app may show you a word again three days after you first learned it, and then again two weeks later.

So don't feel bad when you forget something. Forgetting is not a sign that you are a poor learner. It is a sign that your brain is working normally. The important thing is to review at the right time.

passages.translation:
テストのために一生懸命勉強したのに、1週間後にはほとんど忘れていた、という経験はありませんか。もしそうなら、それはあなただけではありません。忘れることは、脳の働きの自然な一部なのです。

1880年代、ヘルマン・エビングハウスというドイツの科学者が、記憶についての有名な実験をしました。彼は「ZOF」や「BIK」のような意味のない「単語」の一覧を作り、それを覚えようとしました。そして、いろいろな長さの時間がたった後で、どれくらい覚えているかを調べました。その結果は、多くの人を驚かせました。覚えてからわずか20分後には、もう単語の約40パーセントを忘れていました。1日後には、約70パーセントが消えていました。グラフの曲線で表された彼の結果は、今では「忘却曲線」と呼ばれています。

なぜ脳はこんなに早く忘れるのでしょうか。科学者たちは、忘れることは実は役に立っていると考えています。私たちは毎日、ばく大な量の情報を見聞きしています。もしそれをすべて覚えていたら、脳はいっぱいになりすぎて、うまく働かないでしょう。そこで脳は、大切そうな情報だけを残し、残りは捨ててしまうのです。だから、友だちの名前は覚えていても、1か月前の昼食に何を食べたかは覚えていないのです。

では、脳は何が大切かをどのように決めるのでしょうか。大切なしるしの一つは、くり返しです。同じ情報に何度も出会うと、脳は「これは必要だ」と考え、より長く記憶しておきます。エビングハウスは、復習するたびに忘却曲線がゆるやかになることを発見しました。言いかえれば、復習するたびに、私たちはゆっくり忘れるようになるのです。

この考えから、「間隔反復」と呼ばれる学習方法が生まれました。同じ単語を一晩で10回勉強する代わりに、1日後、3日後、1週間後というように復習していくのです。毎回、ちょうど忘れかけるころに復習します。多くの研究で、この方法は一度に全部勉強するよりずっと効果があると示されています。実際、学習アプリの中には、毎日どの単語を復習すべきかを決めるのに、この方法を使っているものもあります。たとえば、アプリは単語を最初に覚えた3日後にもう一度、さらに2週間後にまた見せるかもしれません。

だから、何かを忘れても落ちこむ必要はありません。忘れることは、あなたが学ぶのが下手だというしるしではありません。脳が正常に働いているしるしなのです。大切なのは、ちょうどよいときに復習することです。

passages.title: Grandfather's Camera
passages.body:
Last spring, while Mei was cleaning the storeroom with her mother, she found an old camera in a wooden box. "That was your grandfather's," her mother said. "He loved taking pictures. He took that camera everywhere when he was young." Mei's grandfather had died when she was three, so she did not remember him well.

The camera was not digital. It used film, and there was still a roll of film inside. Mei took it to a small photo shop near the station. The owner, an old man with white hair, looked at the camera and smiled. "I haven't seen one of these for years," he said. He told her that it would take a week to develop the film.

A week later, Mei went back to the shop. The owner handed her an envelope with twenty-four photos in it. Most of them were pictures of flowers and mountains, but the last one was different. It showed a little girl laughing on a swing in a park. In the wooden box, her grandfather had left a small note that said, "Yoko, age 5." Yoko was the name of Mei's mother.

When Mei showed the photo to her mother, her mother was silent for a long time. "I remember this day," she finally said. "Your grandfather took me to the park, and he pushed the swing for an hour. I didn't know that he had taken a picture." Then she said, "If you hadn't found the camera, I would never have seen this photo." Her eyes were full of tears.

After that day, Mei started to use her grandfather's camera. With film, she cannot see her pictures until they are developed, and she can take only twenty-four pictures with one roll. So she thinks carefully before she takes each one. She has learned that waiting can make things more special. Now, whenever she looks through the camera, she feels as if her grandfather were standing next to her.

Last month, Mei took her mother to the same park. She asked her mother to sit on the swing, and she took a picture of her with her grandfather's camera. Her mother laughed and said that she felt like a little girl again. Mei is now waiting for the film to be developed. She hopes that someday her own children will find this photo, just as she found her mother's.

passages.translation:
去年の春、芽衣は母と物置を掃除していて、木の箱に入った古いカメラを見つけました。「それはおじいちゃんのものよ」と母は言いました。「写真を撮るのが大好きでね。若いころは、どこへ行くにもそのカメラを持っていったのよ」芽衣の祖父は彼女が3歳のときに亡くなっていたので、彼女は祖父のことをよく覚えていませんでした。

そのカメラはデジタルではありませんでした。フィルムを使うもので、中にはまだフィルムが1本入っていました。芽衣はそれを、駅の近くの小さな写真店に持っていきました。白髪の年配の店主は、カメラを見てほほえみました。「これは何年も見ていないなあ」と彼は言いました。フィルムを現像するには1週間かかると、彼は言いました。

1週間後、芽衣は店にもどりました。店主は、24枚の写真が入った封筒を手渡しました。ほとんどは花や山の写真でしたが、最後の一枚はちがっていました。それは、公園のブランコに乗って笑っている小さな女の子の写真でした。木の箱の中には、祖父が残した「洋子、5歳」と書かれた小さなメモがありました。洋子は芽衣の母の名前でした。

芽衣が写真を母に見せると、母は長い間だまっていました。「この日のこと、覚えているわ」と、ようやく母は言いました。「おじいちゃんが公園に連れていってくれて、1時間もブランコを押してくれたの。写真を撮っていたなんて知らなかった」それから母は「あなたがカメラを見つけなかったら、この写真を見ることはなかったでしょうね」と言いました。母の目は涙でいっぱいでした。

その日から、芽衣は祖父のカメラを使い始めました。フィルムでは、現像するまで写真を見ることができず、1本で24枚しか撮れません。だから、一枚一枚を撮る前によく考えます。待つことで物事がより特別になることを、彼女は学びました。今では、カメラをのぞくたびに、まるで祖父がとなりに立っているかのように感じます。

先月、芽衣は母を同じ公園へ連れていきました。母にブランコに座ってもらい、祖父のカメラで母の写真を撮りました。母は笑って、また小さな女の子にもどったような気がすると言いました。芽衣は今、フィルムが現像されるのを待っています。ちょうど自分が母の写真を見つけたように、いつか自分の子どもがこの写真を見つけてくれたらいいなと、彼女は思っています。

passages.title: Should We Use AI for Homework?
passages.body:
Today, let's talk about AI, which many of you already use. Some schools allow students to use AI for homework, while others don't. What do you think?

I think AI is very useful. Last week, I didn't understand what my science textbook said about electricity. I asked an AI, and it explained the idea in a way that I could understand easily.

That's a good point, but I'm worried. Some students just copy what AI writes. They don't think by themselves. If they do that, they won't learn anything.

I agree with Lina. AI sometimes gives wrong answers, too. My brother, whose report was written with AI, got a low score because some facts in it were wrong.

Really? I didn't know that. But that's a problem with how people use AI, not with AI itself.

Interesting. Kenji, what do you mean?

A dictionary can be used well or badly, too. If we check the answers AI gives us and think about them, AI can be a good teacher.

Then maybe we need some rules. For example, we should write the first draft by ourselves, and use AI only to check it.

And we should tell our teachers when we use AI. That way, teachers can see what we really did by ourselves.

These are great ideas. The place where we learn is changing quickly, but the purpose of learning is the same. We learn so that we can think for ourselves. Next week, let's make our class rules for AI together.

Can I add one more idea? I think we should also learn how AI makes its answers. If we know that it sometimes mixes up facts, we will be more careful when we use it.

That's true. From now on, I'll check my science answers with my textbook. My father always says, "The person who asks good questions learns the most." Maybe that is what AI can help us with: asking better questions.

I like that idea very much, Kenji. Please think about three rules that you want to suggest, and bring them to class next week.

OK. I'm going to talk with my brother about his report tonight. He may have some good ideas for rules, because he learned a hard lesson.

And I'll ask my parents how they used dictionaries and the internet when they were students. Maybe we can learn something from them, too.

passages.translation:
今日は、みなさんの多くがもう使っているAIについて話しましょう。宿題にAIを使うことを認めている学校もあれば、認めていない学校もあります。みなさんはどう思いますか。

AIはとても役に立つと思います。先週、理科の教科書が電気について言っていることがわかりませんでした。AIに聞いたら、ぼくが簡単にわかるやり方で説明してくれました。

それはいい点だけど、私は心配です。AIが書いたものをそのまま写すだけの生徒もいます。自分で考えないんです。そんなことをしたら、何も身につきません。

ぼくもリナに賛成です。AIはまちがった答えを出すこともあります。ぼくの兄はAIでレポートを書いたのですが、中のいくつかの事実がまちがっていたので、低い点数をとりました。

本当？知らなかった。でも、それはAIそのものではなく、人のAIの使い方の問題だよ。

おもしろいですね。健二さん、どういう意味ですか。

辞書だって、うまくも下手にも使えます。AIがくれる答えを確かめて、それについて考えれば、AIはいい先生になれます。

じゃあ、きまりが必要かもしれません。たとえば、最初の下書きは自分で書いて、AIは確かめるためだけに使う、とか。

それと、AIを使ったときは先生に伝えるべきです。そうすれば、先生はぼくたちが本当に自分でしたことがわかります。

どれもすばらしい考えですね。私たちが学ぶ場は急速に変わっていますが、学ぶ目的は変わりません。私たちは、自分で考えられるようになるために学ぶのです。来週、AIについてのクラスのきまりをいっしょに作りましょう。

もう一つ考えを足してもいいですか。AIがどうやって答えを作るのかも学ぶべきだと思います。AIがときどき事実を取りちがえると知っていれば、使うときにもっと注意するはずです。

確かに。これからは、理科の答えを教科書で確かめるよ。父はいつも「よい質問をする人が、いちばん多くを学ぶ」と言っています。AIが手伝ってくれるのは、もしかしたらそこかもしれません。よりよい質問をすることです。

その考え、とても気に入りました、健二さん。提案したいきまりを3つ考えて、来週の授業に持ってきてください。

わかりました。今夜、兄とレポートのことを話してみます。兄はつらい経験から学んだので、きまりについていい考えがあるかもしれません。

私は、両親が生徒だったころ、辞書やインターネットをどう使っていたか聞いてみます。両親からも何か学べるかもしれません。

passages.title: Where Does Our Electricity Come From?
passages.body:
Electricity is something that we cannot live without. But have you ever thought about where it comes from? For my report, I compared the sources of electricity in Japan in 2010 and 2023. The table shows the results.

In both years, more than half of Japan's electricity came from natural gas and coal. These are fossil fuels, which give off a lot of CO2 when they are burned. In 2023, no other source was used as much as natural gas.

The biggest change was in nuclear power and renewable energy. In 2010, nuclear power made about a quarter of our electricity. After the accident at a nuclear power plant in 2011, many plants were stopped. In 2023, nuclear power made only about eight percent. On the other hand, renewable energy, such as solar, wind, and water power, has grown a lot. In 2023, it made more than twice as much electricity as in 2010.

Renewable energy has good points and bad points. It does not give off CO2, and we will never run out of sunlight or wind. However, the amount of electricity it makes changes with the weather. For example, solar panels cannot make electricity at night. So we need better ways to store electricity, such as large batteries.

The government hopes to make renewable energy a much larger part of our electricity in the future. The more renewable energy we use, the less CO2 we will give off. But that is not only the government's job. We can also save electricity at home by turning off lights and using less air conditioning. Small actions by each of us can make a big difference.

At our school, the science club has started a small project. They put solar panels on the roof of the gym last year. On sunny days, the panels make enough electricity for all the lights in the gym. The members check how much electricity is made every day and put the numbers on the board in the hallway. Since they started, many students have become more interested in energy. I hope that more schools will try projects like this, because learning about energy is the first step to using it wisely. Next year, the club is going to put panels on the roof of the school building, too. I'd like to join the project and learn more about how solar panels work.

passages.translation:
電気は、私たちがなくては生きていけないものです。でも、それがどこから来ているか考えたことはありますか。私はレポートのために、2010年と2023年の日本の電気のもとを比べました。表はその結果です。

どちらの年も、日本の電気の半分以上は天然ガスと石炭から作られました。これらは化石燃料で、燃やすと多くの二酸化炭素を出します。2023年には、天然ガスほど多く使われたものはほかにありませんでした。

いちばん大きな変化は、原子力と再生可能エネルギーでした。2010年、原子力は電気の約4分の1を作っていました。2011年に原子力発電所で事故が起きた後、多くの発電所が止められました。2023年には、原子力は約8パーセントしか作っていません。一方で、太陽光・風力・水力のような再生可能エネルギーは、大きく増えました。2023年には、2010年の2倍以上の電気を作りました。

再生可能エネルギーには、よい点と悪い点があります。二酸化炭素を出さず、太陽の光や風がなくなることは決してありません。しかし、作る電気の量は天気によって変わります。たとえば、太陽光パネルは夜には電気を作れません。だから、大きな電池のような、電気をためるよりよい方法が必要です。

政府は将来、再生可能エネルギーを電気のずっと大きな部分にしたいと考えています。再生可能エネルギーを使えば使うほど、出す二酸化炭素は少なくなります。しかし、それは政府だけの仕事ではありません。私たちも家で、電気を消したり、エアコンをあまり使わないようにしたりして、電気を節約できます。一人一人の小さな行動が、大きな違いを生むのです。

私たちの学校では、科学部が小さなプロジェクトを始めました。去年、体育館の屋根に太陽光パネルを取りつけました。晴れた日には、パネルが体育館のすべての照明に十分な電気を作ります。部員は毎日どれくらいの電気が作られたかを調べ、その数字を廊下の掲示板に貼っています。始めてから、多くの生徒がエネルギーにもっと関心を持つようになりました。エネルギーについて学ぶことは、それを賢く使う第一歩なので、もっと多くの学校がこのようなプロジェクトに挑戦してほしいと思います。来年、科学部は校舎の屋根にもパネルを取りつける予定です。私もそのプロジェクトに参加して、太陽光パネルのしくみをもっと学びたいと思っています。

passages.title: Farms in the City
passages.body:
By 2050, about two out of every three people in the world will live in cities. As cities grow, they need more and more food. But most of the food that city people eat is grown far away in the countryside. It has to travel a long way by truck, ship, or plane before it reaches our tables. This uses a lot of energy, and the food is not always fresh when it arrives.

To solve this problem, some people have started growing food in cities. This is called "urban farming." Some people grow vegetables on the roofs of buildings, and others use empty land between houses. In New York, for example, there is a farm on a roof so large that it produces more than 20,000 kilograms of vegetables a year.

One new kind of urban farm is the "vertical farm." In a vertical farm, plants are grown inside a building on shelves that are stacked high like a bookcase. Instead of sunlight, special LED lights are used. The plants do not need soil, either. Their roots are kept in water that contains everything they need to grow.

Vertical farms have several advantages. First, they can produce food not only in summer but also in winter, because the weather inside never changes. Second, they use about ninety-five percent less water than normal farms, because the water is used again and again. Third, insects cannot get in, so farmers don't have to use chemicals. And because the farms are in the city, vegetables can be sold as soon as they are picked.

However, vertical farms also have a big weak point. The lights and machines use a lot of electricity, so running a vertical farm costs a lot of money. Because of this, most vertical farms grow only vegetables that grow quickly, such as lettuce and herbs. Rice and wheat cannot be grown this way unless the cost of electricity goes down. Some companies are now trying to use solar power so that their farms need less electricity from outside.

Whether urban farming will feed all the world's cities is still not clear. But it shows us that farms do not always have to be in the countryside. It also gives city children a chance to see how vegetables grow. Someday, the salad you eat for lunch may come from a building next to your school.

passages.translation:
2050年までに、世界の人々の約3人に2人が都市に住むようになるでしょう。都市が大きくなるにつれて、ますます多くの食べ物が必要になります。しかし、都市の人々が食べる食べ物のほとんどは、遠くの田舎で育てられています。食卓に届くまでに、トラックや船、飛行機で長い道のりを運ばれなければなりません。これは多くのエネルギーを使いますし、届いたときに食べ物がいつも新鮮とは限りません。

この問題を解決するために、都市で食べ物を育て始めた人々がいます。これは「都市農業」と呼ばれています。ビルの屋上で野菜を育てる人もいれば、家と家の間の空き地を使う人もいます。たとえばニューヨークには、とても広い屋上農園があり、1年に2万キロ以上の野菜を作っています。

新しい種類の都市農園の一つが「垂直農場」です。垂直農場では、植物は建物の中で、本棚のように高く積み重ねられた棚の上で育てられます。太陽の光の代わりに、特別なLEDライトが使われます。植物は土も必要としません。根は、育つのに必要なものがすべて入った水につけられています。

垂直農場にはいくつかの利点があります。第一に、中の天候は決して変わらないので、夏だけでなく冬にも食べ物を作ることができます。第二に、水がくり返し使われるので、ふつうの農場より約95パーセント少ない水ですみます。第三に、虫が入れないので、農家は薬品を使う必要がありません。そして、農場が都市の中にあるので、野菜はとってすぐに売ることができます。

しかし、垂直農場には大きな弱点もあります。照明や機械は多くの電気を使うので、垂直農場の運営にはたくさんのお金がかかります。このため、ほとんどの垂直農場は、レタスやハーブのような早く育つ野菜しか育てていません。電気代が下がらない限り、米や小麦はこの方法では育てられません。今では、外からの電気をあまり必要としないように、太陽光発電を使おうとしている会社もあります。

都市農業が世界のすべての都市を養えるかどうかは、まだはっきりしていません。しかし、それは農場がいつも田舎にある必要はないということを教えてくれます。また、都市の子どもたちに、野菜が育つようすを見る機会を与えてくれます。いつか、あなたが昼食に食べるサラダは、学校のとなりのビルから来るのかもしれません。

passages.title: A Glass Bird from Venice
passages.body:
One Saturday afternoon, Rin was waiting for a train at Ueno Station when an old woman came up to her. The woman showed Rin a piece of paper and said something that Rin couldn't understand. It wasn't English or Japanese. On the paper was the name of a hotel in Asakusa.

Rin asked her in English where she was from. The woman smiled and said that she was from Italy. She knew only a few English words, but she managed to explain that she had lost her way. Rin told her not to worry.

Rin had planned to meet her friends in Shibuya, but she decided to take the woman to her hotel. She sent a message to her friends and told them that she would be late. On the subway, the two of them talked with gestures, pictures on Rin's phone, and a few English words. The woman, whose name was Maria, said that she had come to Japan to see cherry blossoms. She also said that her late husband had always wanted to visit Japan with her.

When they arrived at the hotel, Maria held Rin's hands and said, "Grazie, grazie!" Rin didn't know the word, but she understood what it meant. Maria took a small glass bird out of her bag and gave it to Rin. She explained that it had been made in Venice, her hometown. Rin said that she couldn't take such a beautiful thing, but Maria insisted.

When Rin finally met her friends, she was an hour late. Her friend Kana asked her why she was so late. Rin told them the whole story and showed them the glass bird. Kana said that she would have done the same thing. That night, Rin wrote in her diary, "Language is important, but kindness can be understood without words." The glass bird now sits on her desk, and it reminds her of that day every time she studies English.

A month later, Rin received a postcard from Italy. Maria wrote that she had seen beautiful cherry blossoms in Kyoto and Nara after they said goodbye. She also wrote that she would never forget the kind girl at Ueno Station. Rin decided to write back in English, and she asked her teacher how to write a good letter. Someday, she wants to visit Venice and see the place where the glass bird was made.

sentences.ja: 凛はその言葉を知りませんでしたが、その意味はわかりました。

sentences.en: Maria took a small glass bird out of her bag and gave it to Rin.
sentences.ja: マリアはかばんから小さなガラスの鳥を取り出して、凛にくれました。

sentences.en: She explained that it had been made in Venice, her hometown.
sentences.ja: それは彼女の故郷のベネチアで作られたものだと説明しました。

sentences.en: Rin said that she couldn't take such a beautiful thing, but Maria insisted.
sentences.ja: 凛はそんなにきれいなものはもらえないと言いましたが、マリアはどうしてもと言いました。

sentences.en: When Rin finally met her friends, she was an hour late.
sentences.ja: 凛がようやく友だちと会ったとき、1時間遅れていました。

sentences.en: Her friend Kana asked her why she was so late.
sentences.ja: 友だちの佳奈は、どうしてそんなに遅れたのかとたずねました。

sentences.en: Rin told them the whole story and showed them the glass bird.
sentences.ja: 凛は友だちに一部始終を話し、ガラスの鳥を見せました。

sentences.en: Kana said that she would have done the same thing.
sentences.ja: 佳奈は、自分も同じことをしただろうと言いました。

sentences.en: That night, Rin wrote in her diary, "Language is important, but [[ア=kindness can be understood]] without words."
sentences.ja: その夜、凛は日記に「言葉は大切だけど、親切は言葉がなくても伝わる」と書きました。

sentences.en: The glass bird now sits on her desk, and it reminds her of that day every time she studies English.
sentences.ja: ガラスの鳥は今、凛の机の上にあり、英語を勉強するたびにあの日のことを思い出させてくれます。

sentences.en: A month later, Rin received a postcard from Italy.
sentences.ja: 1か月後、凛はイタリアからはがきを受け取りました。

sentences.en: Maria wrote that she had seen beautiful cherry blossoms in Kyoto and Nara after they said goodbye.
sentences.ja: マリアは、二人が別れた後、京都や奈良で美しい桜を見たと書いていました。

sentences.en: She also wrote that she would never forget the kind girl at Ueno Station.
sentences.ja: 上野駅の親切な女の子のことは決して忘れない、とも書いていました。

sentences.en: Rin decided to write back in English, and she asked her teacher how to write a good letter.
sentences.ja: 凛は英語で返事を書くことにして、先生によい手紙の書き方をたずねました。

sentences.en: Someday, she wants to visit Venice and see the place where the glass bird was made.
sentences.ja: いつかベネチアを訪れて、ガラスの鳥が作られた場所を見たいと、彼女は思っています。

passages.translation:
ある土曜日の午後、凛が上野駅で電車を待っていると、一人の年配の女性が近づいてきました。女性は凛に一枚の紙を見せ、凛にはわからない何かを言いました。それは英語でも日本語でもありませんでした。紙には、浅草のホテルの名前が書いてありました。

凛は英語で、どこから来たのかとたずねました。女性はほほえんで、イタリアから来たと言いました。彼女は英語を少ししか知りませんでしたが、道に迷ってしまったことを、なんとか説明しました。凛は彼女に、心配しないでと言いました。

凛は渋谷で友だちと会う予定でしたが、その女性をホテルまで連れていくことにしました。彼女は友だちにメッセージを送り、遅れると伝えました。地下鉄の中で、二人は身ぶりや凛のスマートフォンの写真、少しの英語で話しました。マリアという名前のその女性は、桜を見に日本へ来たのだと言いました。また、亡くなった夫が、いつも彼女といっしょに日本を訪れたがっていたとも言いました。

ホテルに着くと、マリアは凛の手をにぎって「グラッツィエ、グラッツィエ！」と言いました。凛はその言葉を知りませんでしたが、その意味はわかりました。マリアはかばんから小さなガラスの鳥を取り出して、凛にくれました。それは彼女の故郷のベネチアで作られたものだと説明しました。凛はそんなにきれいなものはもらえないと言いましたが、マリアはどうしてもと言いました。

凛がようやく友だちと会ったとき、1時間遅れていました。友だちの佳奈は、どうしてそんなに遅れたのかとたずねました。凛は友だちに一部始終を話し、ガラスの鳥を見せました。佳奈は、自分も同じことをしただろうと言いました。その夜、凛は日記に「言葉は大切だけど、親切は言葉がなくても伝わる」と書きました。ガラスの鳥は今、凛の机の上にあり、英語を勉強するたびにあの日のことを思い出させてくれます。

1か月後、凛はイタリアからはがきを受け取りました。マリアは、二人が別れた後、京都や奈良で美しい桜を見たと書いていました。上野駅の親切な女の子のことは決して忘れない、とも書いていました。凛は英語で返事を書くことにして、先生によい手紙の書き方をたずねました。いつかベネチアを訪れて、ガラスの鳥が作られた場所を見たいと、彼女は思っています。

passages.title: Smartphones and Sleep
passages.body:
Our school health committee did a survey of 300 students about their smartphone use and sleep. We asked them how many hours they used their smartphones each day and how many hours they slept at night. The graph shows the average hours of sleep for each group.

The graph clearly shows that the longer students use their smartphones, the shorter they sleep. Students who use them for less than one hour a day sleep about 8.3 hours. Those who use them for more than four hours sleep only about 6.5 hours. That is almost two hours less. Doctors say that junior high school students need eight to ten hours of sleep, so most groups are not sleeping enough.

However, this does not always mean that smartphones are the only reason for short sleep. Some students told us that they had a lot of homework and went to bed late. Others said that they used their phones because they couldn't sleep. In other words, short sleep might be a cause, not a result, of using phones at night.

Still, it is true that the light from screens makes it harder to fall asleep. Not only does the light tell our brains that it is still daytime, but games and messages also keep our minds active. Never have I seen my older brother put his phone down before midnight! He often says that he is tired in the morning, but he doesn't think that his phone is the reason.

Our committee made three suggestions. First, stop using your phone at least thirty minutes before bed. Second, keep your phone outside your bedroom at night. Third, if you can't sleep, read a paper book instead. It was not until we did this survey that we realized how much sleep we were losing. We hope that every student will try at least one of these ideas this week.

After we shared these results at a school assembly, some students started a "no-phone hour" before bed. One of them told us that she now falls asleep faster and feels better in the morning. Even my brother has agreed to try it for one week. We are planning to do the same survey again next spring to see whether things have changed. If you have any good ideas for better sleep, please tell our committee.

passages.translation:
学校の保健委員会は、300人の生徒にスマートフォンの使用と睡眠について調査をしました。1日に何時間スマートフォンを使うか、夜に何時間眠るかをたずねました。グラフは、グループごとの平均睡眠時間を示しています。

グラフは、生徒がスマートフォンを長く使うほど、睡眠が短くなることをはっきり示しています。1日1時間未満しか使わない生徒は、約8.3時間眠っています。4時間以上使う生徒は、約6.5時間しか眠っていません。ほぼ2時間少ないのです。医者は中学生には8〜10時間の睡眠が必要だと言っているので、ほとんどのグループは睡眠が足りていません。

しかし、これはスマートフォンだけが短い睡眠の原因だということを、必ずしも意味するわけではありません。宿題が多くて遅く寝るのだと話してくれた生徒もいました。眠れないからスマートフォンを使うのだと言う生徒もいました。言いかえれば、短い睡眠は、夜にスマートフォンを使うことの結果ではなく、原因なのかもしれません。

それでも、画面の光が寝つきにくくするのは本当です。その光が脳にまだ昼間だと伝えるだけでなく、ゲームやメッセージも頭を活発にさせ続けます。私は、兄が真夜中より前にスマートフォンを置くのを、一度も見たことがありません！兄はよく朝は疲れていると言いますが、スマートフォンが原因だとは思っていません。

私たちの委員会は、3つの提案をしました。第一に、寝る少なくとも30分前には、スマートフォンを使うのをやめること。第二に、夜はスマートフォンを寝室の外に置くこと。第三に、眠れないときは、代わりに紙の本を読むこと。この調査をして初めて、私たちはどれだけ睡眠を失っているかに気づきました。すべての生徒が、今週、少なくともこのうち一つを試してくれることを願っています。

全校集会でこの結果を伝えた後、寝る前に「スマートフォンを使わない1時間」を始めた生徒もいます。そのうちの一人は、今は前より早く寝つけて、朝の気分もよくなったと話してくれました。兄でさえ、1週間試してみることに賛成しました。何か変わったかどうかを確かめるため、来年の春にも同じ調査をする予定です。よく眠るためのよい考えがあれば、ぜひ委員会に教えてください。

passages.title: My Friend Tom
passages.body:
This is my friend Tom. He is from Australia, and he lives in Saitama with his family. He is fourteen years old. He is in my class.

Tom likes sports very much. He plays soccer after school. He can run very fast. In his town in Australia, December is summer. So he doesn't like cold winter days in Japan.

Tom speaks English and a little Japanese. He studies Japanese every day. His favorite Japanese word is "oishii." He often eats rice balls for lunch.

On Sundays, Tom and I go to the library. I help him with Japanese, and he helps me with English. We are good friends.

passages.title: Lunch Before the Movie
passages.body:
Hello. What would you like?

I'd like a sandwich and orange juice, please.

Which sandwich would you like, egg or ham?

Egg, please. How much is it?

It's 600 yen.

I want a hamburger. Can I have a cola, too?

Sorry, we don't have cola. We have tea and apple juice.

OK. Apple juice, please.

The hamburger is 700 yen, and the juice is 300 yen.

Here you are. Mai, what time is it now?

It's 12:30. The movie starts at 1:15.

Good. We have time. Let's eat here. This shop is near the movie theater.

OK. And let's buy some popcorn at the theater, too. I love popcorn!

passages.title: Clubs at Our School
passages.body:
I'm Rina, and I'm in the art club. This table shows the clubs at our school. How many members does each club have? Please look at the table.

The brass band has thirty members. It practices six days a week. The members play music at school events. The brass band is very popular, and its concert is in July every year.

The art club has twelve members. We meet on Tuesdays and Fridays. I like drawing pictures of flowers.

The science club has only nine members. But the members do fun experiments every week. Do you like science? Please come and see the science club!

figure.title: Clubs at Midori Junior High School

passages.translation:
私は里奈で、美術部に入っています。この表は、私たちの学校の部活動を示しています。それぞれの部には何人の部員がいるでしょうか。表を見てください。

吹奏楽部には30人の部員がいます。週に6日練習します。部員は学校の行事で音楽を演奏します。吹奏楽部はとても人気があり、毎年7月にコンサートがあります。

美術部には12人の部員がいます。私たちは火曜日と金曜日に集まります。私は花の絵をかくのが好きです。

科学部には部員が9人しかいません。でも、部員は毎週おもしろい実験をします。あなたは理科が好きですか。ぜひ科学部を見に来てください！

passages.title: Grandpa and Pochi
passages.body:
My grandfather lives near my house. He has a dog. Its name is Pochi. Pochi is white and very big.

Every morning, Grandpa gets up at five. He takes Pochi to the river. They walk for an hour. Grandpa says, "This walk is good for Pochi and me."

On Saturdays, I go with them. Pochi runs to the river and swims. Grandpa doesn't swim, but he watches Pochi with a smile. I play with Pochi, and we have a good time.

Pochi is old now. He doesn't run fast. But he is still a very good friend for Grandpa. Grandpa often says to Pochi, "You are my family."
